title: Writing for the Board
briefing: The quarterly risk report goes to the board in two weeks. Last quarter's ran to 46 pages; the chair, Dame Helen Oyelaran (non-executive, ex-regulator), said she couldn't find what mattered.

context.text: The chair knows about the breach that was once left out of a committee report. She will read this one closely.
The refrigerant transition risk you added is now the chair's favourite question.

evidence.title: Last quarter's report
evidence.body: 46 pages. Section order: methodology, unit registers, KRIs (82 charts), actions (114 rows). The two appetite breaches were on pages 31 and 38.

evidence.title: This quarter's position
evidence.body: Two enterprise risks deteriorated (people; cold-chain integrity). One appetite breach (driver hours). Coldline 2 back on track. One near-miss involving a pharma load.

evidence.title: Chair's note
evidence.body: "Tell me what has changed, what is outside appetite, what you need us to decide, and what you are worried about that isn't in the numbers."

options.label: What changed, what is outside appetite, decisions needed, and your judgement on emerging concerns
options.feedback: Exactly what the chair asked for.

options.label: The methodology and scales first, so the board can trust and interpret the numbers that follow
Progress this quarter (Coldline 2, actions closed), so the board sees the risk function delivering
options.feedback: Good news belongs in the report but not at the top.

questions.prompt: Where does the driver-hours appetite breach go?

options.label: On page one, with the owner's plan and expected return date
options.feedback: Breaches are the board's business; they lead.

options.label: In the KRI section with the other indicators, clearly marked red
options.feedback: Last time that put breaches on page 31.

options.label: Raised verbally by the COO at the meeting, so he can explain the context in person
options.feedback: Breaches must be on the record.

questions.prompt: What do you put under 'what we're worried about that isn't in the numbers'?

options.label: The pharma near miss as a sign of fragility as volumes grow, and engineer shortages KRIs miss
options.feedback: Judgement the board can't get from charts.

options.label: Nothing: the report should stick to measured facts the board can rely on
options.feedback: The chair asked explicitly for your judgement.

options.label: A full list of the emerging risks from the horizon scan, so nothing is left out of the board's view
options.feedback: Shows nothing about what you actually think.

questions.prompt: Which decision do you put to the board?

options.label: Approve a 0.6m engineer apprenticeship programme for the people risk on the profile
options.feedback: A clear, costed decision tied to a deteriorating enterprise risk.

options.label: None: the report is for information, and board decisions belong in separate papers
options.feedback: Boards are there to decide; give them the decision.

options.label: Ask the board to approve the full action plan of 114 items as one decision

questions.prompt: How long should the main report be?

options.label: About 6-8 pages, with registers, KRI detail and method in appendices
options.feedback: Short enough to read, complete enough to trust.

options.label: A one-page dashboard only, with the full pack available on request
options.feedback: Too thin for the board to discharge its oversight.

options.label: Keep the full 46 pages but add a contents page so directors can navigate

lesson: Board reporting leads with change, breaches, decisions and judgement. Detail goes to appendices; the board's time goes to what it must decide.
